ig_caption:
New York, 1956. At the Rosenwald tournament, 13-year-old Bobby Fischer had Black against Donald Byrne, one of the leading American players.

On move 11 Fischer put a knight where it could be taken. On move 17 he left his queen to be captured and moved a bishop instead. What followed was a 'windmill': check after check from a knight and bishop, collecting White's pieces one by one. By move 25 Black had two rooks, two bishops and a knight against a queen, and Fischer finished with mate on move 41. A magazine of the day called it the Game of the Century, and the name stuck.

Would you have left the queen? 👇

Slide 2: New York, 1956. Board after 11...Na4: Fischer puts his knight where White's knight can take it.
Slide 3: The queen stays put. Board after 17.Kf1 Be6: Black ignores the attack on the queen on b6.
Slide 4: The windmill. Board after 25...Nxd1: checks from knight and bishop help Black win back far more than the queen.
Slide 5: Mate with the little pieces. Board after 41...Rc2 mate: rook, bishops and knight trap White's king.

slides.title: New York, 1956
slides.moves: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4
slides.take: Donald Byrne, White, against Bobby Fischer, aged 13. On move 11 Fischer puts a knight on a4, where White's knight can take it.
slides.edge: Taking it would let Black grab the e4 pawn and start an attack. Byrne moves his queen to a3 instead.

slides.title: The queen stays put
slides.moves: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4 Qa3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Bxe7 Qb6 Bc4 Nxc3 Bc5 Rfe8+ Kf1 Be6
slides.take: White's bishop attacks Black's queen on b6. Instead of moving it, Fischer plays 17...Be6 and offers it.
slides.edge: The bishop now hits White's bishop on c4, and White's king on f1 is still stuck in the middle.

slides.title: The windmill
slides.moves: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4 Qa3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Bxe7 Qb6 Bc4 Nxc3 Bc5 Rfe8+ Kf1 Be6 Bxb6 Bxc4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nxd4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nc3+ Kg1 axb6 Qb4 Ra4 Qxb6 Nxd1
slides.take: After 18.Bxb6, checks from knight and bishop win a pawn. Black takes back the bishop, then the knight takes the rook on d1.
slides.edge: Now Black has two rooks, two bishops and a knight. White has a queen, a rook and a knight.

slides.title: Mate with the little pieces
slides.moves: Nf3 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 d4 O-O Bf4 d5 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 c6 e4 Nbd7 Rd1 Nb6 Qc5 Bg4 Bg5 Na4 Qa3 Nxc3 bxc3 Nxe4 Bxe7 Qb6 Bc4 Nxc3 Bc5 Rfe8+ Kf1 Be6 Bxb6 Bxc4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nxd4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nc3+ Kg1 axb6 Qb4 Ra4 Qxb6 Nxd1 h3 Rxa2 Kh2 Nxf2 Re1 Rxe1 Qd8+ Bf8 Nxe1 Bd5 Nf3 Ne4 Qb8 b5 h4 h5 Ne5 Kg7 Kg1 Bc5+ Kf1 Ng3+ Ke1 Bb4+ Kd1 Bb3+ Kc1 Ne2+ Kb1 Nc3+ Kc1 Rc2#
slides.take: White's queen is far away on b8. 41...Rc2 is mate: rook, two bishops and knight surround the king.
slides.edge: A queen is worth a lot. A team of pieces near the king can be worth more.
